event.title: A manager-free channel shares a screenshot of your boss
event.description: In the Lynx late-night Slack channel, where no managers are allowed, someone posts a screenshot of Chris tearing into people: "If you can't even do this, what bonus do you think you deserve?" The next message: "Thoughts? Should we reply as a group?" You're in the channel. Passing a copy to HR, a staff representative, a union or a solicitor so they can deal with the complaint is not itself a disciplinary matter. Spreading it to people who have nothing to do with the complaint is another matter.

chosen.action: Message Chris privately about team morale, without saying how you know

common_unexecuted.action: Ask them to stop spreading it, keep the evidence the target needs, and raise it through a grievance or staff rep

event.title: A colleague who keeps handing you his work

event.title: Raising a technical objection on another team's API design
event.description: While reviewing a downstream API design from a neighbouring team, your own load tests flag a likely bottleneck: at peak, once QPS doubles, tail latency could jump from 50ms to around 800ms and threaten your SLA. How you raise it will decide whether the design actually changes.

event.title: Emergency hotfix — do you skip the process?
event.description: Production has a critical fault and needs an immediate hotfix. The standard path of code review, staging checks and a confirmed rollback would take about two hours. A client is in the middle of a live promotional stream, and every minute of downtime is a serious loss. The operations lead hints you could ship now and backfill the process later.

chosen.action: Ship on a shortened path while the team prepares a rollback and completes the review within an hour

common_unexecuted.action: Stick to the full process, and turn on a degraded mode to limit the impact on the client

event.title: Raising a technical objection on another team's API design
event.description: While reviewing a downstream API design from a neighbouring team, your own load tests flag a likely bottleneck: at peak, once QPS doubles, tail latency could jump from 50ms to around 800ms and threaten your SLA. Their design has already passed their internal review. The owner is a well-regarded senior engineer. Formal integration starts next Wednesday, so there is little time to talk it through. How you raise it will decide whether the design actually changes.

chosen.action: Take their owner aside for a 1:1 and walk through the load-test results privately

common_unexecuted.action: Comment publicly on the shared design doc, with the load-test data attached

event.title: Your idea is pitched first by someone else
event.description: In a team brainstorm you suggest a design, but it gets little attention. Two weeks later a colleague pitches almost the same idea in a wider meeting, with some of the same wording. A VP likes it and asks them to lead it. You cannot tell whether they got there independently or borrowed yours. Either way, they are now seen as the person who proposed it and will take most of the credit.

chosen.action: Share your earlier thinking with the team, without directly challenging their claim to the idea

common_unexecuted.action: Speak to them privately afterwards, mention the discussion two weeks ago, and check where the idea came from

event.title: A manager-free channel shares a screenshot of your boss
event.description: In the Lynx late-night Slack channel, where no managers are allowed, someone posts a screenshot of Chris tearing into people: "If you can't even do this, what bonus do you think you deserve?" The next message: "Thoughts? Should we reply as a group?" You're in the channel. Passing a copy to HR, a staff representative, a union or a solicitor so they can deal with the complaint is not itself a disciplinary matter. Spreading it to people who have nothing to do with the complaint is another matter.

chosen.action: Message Chris privately about team morale, without saying how you know

common_unexecuted.action: Ask them to stop spreading it, keep the evidence the target needs, and raise it through a grievance or staff rep

event.title: Peer review finds a serious bug in a friend's code
event.description: Craig, a colleague you get on well with, has an SQL injection risk in his merge request. He messages privately: “Merge it for now — I'll buy dinner tonight and fix it after.”

chosen.action: Merge it and help him fix it this evening

common_unexecuted.action: Block the review and require a fix before merge

event.title: Thanking a colleague from the next team who went out of their way
event.description: Last week a nasty bug in a barely maintained legacy submodule had you stuck for two days. Chris, a senior engineer on the next team, sat at your desk for a whole afternoon and helped you find and fix it. Nobody required them to spend that long. It is Friday, and you want to say thank you. You could take them out for a good lunch on you, around £30–40. You could write a formal recognition note on the intranet, copied to Chris and their manager, recording their high-quality cross-team help. Or you could do nothing special now and make a point of helping them next time they need it.

chosen.action: Do nothing special for now and help them next time they need it

common_unexecuted.action: Write a formal recognition note and copy their manager

event.title: Whether to invest in a CI automation suite
event.description: Your team still lacks a proper automated-test CI pipeline. Every release depends on senior engineers manually reviewing critical paths. Your manager wants you to lead the platform work. Headcount has just doubled from five to ten. New joiners' PRs have piled up, review pressure has spiked, and releases are starting to slip. Building a CI suite from scratch, with mocks, load tests and coverage gates, would take about two solid weeks, and two of your scheduled projects would slip in that time. Your manager is not insisting on it, so the call is yours.

chosen.action: Keep manual review and let new joiners follow the existing process

common_unexecuted.action: Spend two weeks building a full CI automation suite

event.title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend

The team's culture is fairly direct, and HR has just started talking about psychological safety.

chosen.action: Approve it, and explain on Slack afterwards

common_unexecuted.action: Name the problem directly and mark it as must-fix

chosen.action: Refactor in stages on the current architecture
